idiom_name: map[string]Symbol per scope with a parent-linked *Scope
implementation_notes: Go collapses the classic structure into built-ins: a map[string]Symbol per scope plus a parent-linked *Scope (or a []*Scope used as a stack) with Define and Lookup methods is the whole table, and interning identifiers in a map[string]uint32 keeps keys small when later phases want symbol ids. What replaces the classic entry and table classes is the built-in map plus the slice; the language has no exceptions, so duplicate and unresolved findings are returned as bool/error results instead of thrown. Keep the hand-written chain for your own language or DSL; when the language being analysed is Go itself, the standard library already ships the table - go/types.Scope has Lookup, position-aware LookupParent (innermost outward) and Innermost, and types.Info.Scopes maps AST nodes to their scopes after type checking - which is the second variant.
pitfalls: Go maps are reference types: copying a Scope value shares the underlying map, so scopes must be passed as pointers (or Define must have a pointer receiver) to keep exactly one table per scope.
A nil map write panics: a Scope built as a struct literal without make fails at the first Define, so always construct through the constructor.

go/types resolves Go source, not your language: using it means feeding go/ast trees through types.Config.Check and reading types.Info.Scopes; it is not a generic symbol-table library and gives Go's errors, not yours.

variants.name: go/types Scope tree for Go source
variants.implementation_notes: For Go source the standard library supplies the pattern: parser.ParseFile builds the AST, types.Config.Check builds the tables, and the resulting *types.Package plus types.Info expose scopes - Scope.Lookup searches only one scope, Scope.LookupParent walks outward returning the first object visible from a position, Scope.Innermost finds the scope containing a position, and Info.Scopes maps AST nodes to their scopes. What replaces the classic structure is the Go type checker's own scope tree (Universe -> package -> file -> function -> block), which encodes block scoping, imports and package scope correctly and is maintained by the Go team. The cost is that it type-checks Go only, requires the full go/types input pipeline (parser, token.FileSet, importer), and reports Go's diagnostics rather than your language's.
variants.code_sketch:
fset := token.NewFileSet()
f, _ := parser.ParseFile(fset, "x.go", src, 0)
info := &types.Info{Scopes: map[ast.Node]*types.Scope{}}
conf := types.Config{Importer: importer.Default()}
pkg, _ := conf.Check("x", fset, []*ast.File{f}, info)
scope := info.Scopes[f]                      // file scope of the file
_, obj := scope.LookupParent("x", pos)       // innermost outward from pos
pitfalls: Scopes are populated only after Check returns and only for nodes the checker recorded in types.Info: reading them mid-check yields nil maps.

Scope.Lookup and LookupParent do not model all of Go's binding rules on their own (dot-imports, universe scope and the special any alias are handled inside the checker), so using them outside Check produces subtly different answers.
